title: Personal Narrative
tagline: Tell a true story that means something.
summary: You will communicate a meaningful personal experience using narrative structure, purposeful details, audience awareness, and expressive delivery.
whyItMatters: Stories are how people make sense of experience. College essays, job interviews, and community meetings all reward people who can tell a short, true story that shows who they are and why something matters.

hs: Choose a personal experience with a clear point or significance.
Organize the story with a beginning, conflict, turning point, and resolution.
Use specific sensory details and vivid language.
Deliver with eye contact, vocal variety, and purposeful pauses.
college: Select and frame a personal experience so its significance connects to a broader audience.
Structure narrative tension deliberately and justify structural choices.
Apply language standards for clarity and vividness from Chapter 10.
Evaluate how ethos is built through self-disclosure and audience adaptation.

steps.title: Find your story
steps.detail: List moments that changed how you think, what you value, or what you do. Pick one you are comfortable sharing with this audience.

steps.title: Name the significance
steps.detail: Finish this sentence: "This story matters because..." Your answer becomes your central idea.

steps.title: Map the arc
steps.detail: Use the story arc builder to plan the beginning, conflict, turning point, and resolution.

steps.title: Choose details
steps.detail: Keep the details that help the audience see, hear, and feel the key moments. Cut the rest.

steps.title: Frame it
steps.detail: Write an opening that pulls listeners into the moment and a closing that returns to the significance.

steps.title: Rehearse
steps.detail: Practice out loud with a timer. Mark places to pause before the turning point and after the resolution.

tools.title: Story arc builder
tools.intro: Fill each stage. The arc rises as your story takes shape.

tools.title: Sensory detail workshop
tools.intro: Pick the single most important moment in your story and describe it through the senses. Keep only the details that serve the story.

fields.label: The key moment
fields.help: One sentence: where are you and what is happening?

fields.label: Rewrite one plain sentence vividly
fields.help: Example: "I was nervous" → "My hands left damp prints on the audition sheet."

fields.label: What changed in you because of this experience?
fields.frame: Before this, I thought... Afterward, I realized...

fields.label: Why might your audience care?
fields.frame: Many people my age have experienced...

fields.label: Your central idea in one sentence

tools.title: Rehearse with the timer
tools.intro: Time your story and practice purposeful pauses.
tools.label: Open the Delivery Lab

topicIdeas: A time you were wrong about someone
The first time you did something hard
A tradition in your family and what it means
A moment you stood up for yourself or someone else
An object that holds a story
A failure that taught you something

structures.name: Classic arc
outline: Opening: drop the audience into a moment
Beginning: who, where, what was normal
Conflict: what went wrong or what was at stake
Turning point: the moment things changed

structures.name: Frame story
outline: Present day: a scene that echoes the past

checklist: My story has one clear significance.
I can tell it within the time limit.
The conflict and turning point are easy to identify.
I use at least three specific sensory details.
I pause before the turning point.
I make eye contact during the most important moment.
My conclusion returns to the significance.
I am comfortable sharing every detail with this audience.
reflection: Which moment in your story got the strongest reaction? Why?
What detail would you add or cut next time?
How did telling a personal story feel compared with other speeches?
collegeExtension: Write a one-page rationale analyzing your structural and language choices with reference to Chapters 7 and 10, and explain how you managed ethos through self-disclosure.

title: Informative Speech
tagline: Teach your audience something worth knowing.
summary: You will develop an organized, evidence-based presentation that teaches an audience something meaningful, clearly and accurately.
whyItMatters: Explaining complex ideas clearly is one of the most valued skills in school and work: training a coworker, presenting research, or helping your community understand a change.

hs: Choose a focused topic that is new or useful to the audience.
Write a clear specific purpose and central idea.
Organize two to five main points using an appropriate pattern.
Support ideas with credible, cited sources.
Design a presentation aid that improves understanding.
college: Distinguish informative content from opinion and avoid disguised persuasion.
Select an organizational pattern suited to the type of informative speech (Section 12.2).
Integrate varied supporting materials with accurate oral and written citations (APA or as assigned).
Adapt technical content for a nonexpert audience using definitions, examples, and analogies.
Design presentation aids using principles from Section 9.4.

steps.title: Explore topics
steps.detail: Use the topic explorer to connect your interests with what your audience would find new or useful.

steps.title: Focus
steps.detail: Write a specific purpose ("To inform my audience...") and a one-sentence central idea.

steps.title: Research
steps.detail: Find credible sources. Note author, date, and how you will cite each one out loud.

steps.title: Organize
steps.detail: Choose a pattern and draft two to five main points.

steps.title: Develop
steps.detail: Add supporting material, connectives, an introduction, and a conclusion.

steps.title: Design aids
steps.detail: Create one or more presentation aids that show what words alone cannot.

steps.title: Rehearse
steps.detail: Practice extemporaneously from speaking notes and time each run.

tools.title: Informative topic explorer
tools.intro: Section 12.2 describes five types of informative speeches. Brainstorm one idea for each, then choose.

fields.label: Biography: a person's life or contribution

checklist: My specific purpose begins with "To inform" and contains one idea.
My central idea is a complete declarative sentence.
My speech has two to five main points in a clear pattern.
I cite each source out loud with author or organization and date.
I define terms my audience may not know.
I use connectives between main points.
My presentation aid is readable from the back of the room.

reflection: What will your audience remember most? Why?
Which source was most useful, and how did you verify it?
Which part of your organization would you change?
collegeExtension: Submit a full preparation outline with APA (or assigned style) references and a one-paragraph audience analysis explaining how you adapted technical content for nonexperts.

title: Persuasive Speech
tagline: Make a researched case that moves people.
summary: You will build a researched argument designed to influence an audience's beliefs, attitudes, or actions, ethically and with sound reasoning.
whyItMatters: Civic life, advocacy, and leadership depend on people who can make honest, well-supported arguments and respond fairly to disagreement.

hs: Write a clear proposition (claim) for a short classroom speech.
Support the claim with credible evidence and explain the reasoning.
Use ethos, pathos, and logos appropriately.
Address a counterargument fairly.
End with a specific call to action.
college: Identify the proposition type (fact, definition, value, policy) and choose a matching organizational pattern.
Analyze the audience's position on the persuasion continuum and set a realistic goal.
Evaluate the reasoning behind each main point and avoid logical fallacies.
Integrate and cite academic sources, including at least one that challenges your position.
Apply ethical standards for persuasion from Chapters 3 and 13.

steps.title: Explore
steps.detail: Pick an issue you care about where reasonable people disagree and your audience can actually do something.

steps.title: Claim
steps.detail: Write your proposition and identify its type.

steps.title: Analyze the audience
steps.detail: Where are they on the persuasion continuum? What would make them skeptical?

steps.title: Build the case
steps.detail: Gather evidence for each reason and explain the reasoning that connects them.

steps.title: Answer objections
steps.detail: State the strongest counterargument fairly, then respond with evidence.

steps.title: Organize
steps.detail: Use problem-solution, problem-cause-solution, or Monroe's Motivated Sequence.

steps.title: Check reasoning
steps.detail: Test your own argument for fallacies.

steps.title: Close
steps.detail: Write a specific, doable call to action and rehearse.

fields.label: For your top choice: what do reasonable people disagree about?
What could your audience actually do about it?

tools.title: Claim and evidence builder
tools.intro: Claim, evidence, reasoning: each reason needs all three.

fields.label: Exactly what should the audience do?

Final line
fields.help: Return to your opening story, a vivid image of the future, or a challenge.

topicIdeas: Our school should offer a financial literacy course
Teens should register as organ donors when eligible

structures.name: Problem-solution
outline: I. The problem and its significance
II. The solution and why it works

structures.name: Problem-cause-solution
outline: III. A solution that addresses the causes

checklist: My proposition is clear and I know its type.
Every reason has evidence and an explanation of the reasoning.
I cite each source out loud.
I address at least one counterargument fairly.
I checked my argument for fallacies.
My emotional appeals are honest and proportionate.
My call to action is specific and doable.
I finish within the time limit.
reflection: Which reason was most persuasive to your audience? How can you tell?
How fairly did you represent the other side?
What would you change about your call to action?
collegeExtension: Include an annotated reference list with at least one source that challenges your position, and a paragraph explaining your placement of the rebuttal using your audience analysis.

title: Special Occasion Speech
tagline: Find the right words for a moment that matters.
summary: You will explore communication for meaningful occasions such as celebrations, tributes, introductions, commemorations, and ceremonies.
whyItMatters: Toasts, eulogies, award acceptances, and introductions are the speeches most people give most often in life. Doing them well honors people and brings communities together.

hs: Identify the type of occasion and what the audience expects.
Choose a tone and language that fit the occasion.
Organize a short tribute or ceremonial speech.
Deliver with sincerity and appropriate emotion.
college: Distinguish special occasion speeches from research-based speeches (Section 15.1).
Use evocative language techniques from Section 15.3 and Chapter 10 with purpose.
Adapt to occasion, audience, and time constraints.
Analyze a published ceremonial speech and apply its strategies.

steps.title: Choose the occasion
steps.detail: Use the occasion selector to identify your speech type and what the audience expects.

steps.title: Know your subject
steps.detail: Gather true, specific details about the person, group, or event you are honoring.

steps.title: Set the tone
steps.detail: Decide on the balance of warmth, humor, and seriousness.

steps.title: Organize
steps.detail: Use the tribute organizer to build a short, focused structure.

steps.title: Polish the language
steps.detail: Add one or two memorable phrases using repetition, imagery, or parallelism.

steps.title: Rehearse
steps.detail: Practice until you can deliver emotional moments steadily.

title: Introductory Speech
summary: A short first speech that builds comfort with the audience while practicing basic structure.
whyItMatters: First impressions in class, clubs, and interviews often start with a short self-introduction.

hs: Organize a short speech with an introduction, body, and conclusion.
Share specific details instead of general statements.
Practice eye contact and a steady pace.
college: Apply the five elements of an introduction to a short speech.
Use one artifact or story to create a unifying theme.

steps.title: Choose a theme
steps.detail: Pick an object, place, or word that represents you.

steps.title: Select three details
steps.detail: Each should connect to the theme.

steps.title: Frame and rehearse
steps.detail: Open with the theme, close by returning to it.

title: Demonstration Speech
summary: An informative process speech in which you demonstrate the steps while explaining them.
whyItMatters: Training others, teaching skills, and presenting products all rely on clear demonstrations.

hs: Break a process into clear, ordered steps.
Use objects or visuals effectively.
Explain while demonstrating.
college: Apply chronological organization and connectives to a process.
Plan presentation aids that remain visible and safe.

steps.detail: Pick something you can show in the time limit.

steps.title: List steps
steps.detail: Group small steps into three to five stages.

steps.title: Plan materials

title: Impromptu Speech
summary: A short speech with little or no preparation time, built from a quick structure.
whyItMatters: Interviews, meetings, and class discussions often require organized answers on the spot.

hs: Organize a response quickly using a simple structure.
Stay calm and finish with a clear point.
college: Apply the strengths and limits of impromptu delivery described in Section 11.2.
Use a consistent structure across varied prompts.

steps.detail: Answer the prompt in one sentence.

title: Group Presentation
summary: A team presentation that requires shared planning, clear roles, and smooth handoffs.
whyItMatters: Most workplaces present as teams. Coordination is a communication skill.

hs: Divide responsibilities fairly.
Create one unified introduction and conclusion.
Plan transitions between speakers.
college: Apply the guidance for group informative speeches in Section 12.5.
Evaluate group process as well as product.

steps.title: Agree on purpose
steps.detail: Write one shared specific purpose and central idea.

steps.title: Assign roles
steps.detail: Divide research, speaking, and design.

steps.title: Plan handoffs
steps.detail: Write a connective for each transition between speakers.

steps.title: Rehearse together
steps.detail: Practice at least once as a full group, timed.

title: College Public Speaking Capstone
summary: A culminating speech that demonstrates research, organization, rhetorical analysis, ethical persuasion, and polished delivery.
whyItMatters: A capstone shows growth across the course and prepares you for academic and professional presentations.

college: Conduct and cite academic research in the assigned style.

Adapt to a defined audience using formal audience analysis.
Deliver extemporaneously with purposeful aids.
Reflect critically on growth using earlier self-assessments.
